The town name Inverleigh, Hamilton Highway at Dawber Road and Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve each have 3. The reserve is a minor share compared with the town and the river.

**Sacred Kingfisher** *Todiramphus sanctus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 
- trees: Sacred Kingfishers perch on a low branch and nest in a hollow, a termite mound or a river bank. Birds in Backyards says they inhabit woodland, tall open eucalypt forest, and also mangroves, paperbark forest and melaleuca forest, and that both sexes excavate a burrow in a termite mound, a hollow branch or a river bank. They take insects, reptiles and crustaceans, and only occasionally fish, by sallying from a low exposed branch. Wikipedia adds river and lake margins, wetlands, farmland, parks and gardens, and says southern birds move north after breeding. Mangroves and paperbarks are part of the national account and are not described for Inverleigh. The local match is River Red Gum woodland along the Leigh and Barwon, and Manna Gum and River Red Gum in the reserve. No local record names the nest site.
- hangouts: Within 5 km of Inverleigh, the Atlas of Living Australia holds 113 records of this species. The largest public strings are Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve (21), the town name Inverleigh (11), the Leigh River south of the Hamilton Highway (9), the Barwon–Leigh junction (8), Lawson Reserve (5) and Barwon River at Olivers Property (4). Links Track in the reserve has 3, and Barwon River at Bell Bridge has 2. Birds in Backyards says southern birds leave in winter. These ALA records are not split by month here.

- trees: Rainbow Lorikeets feed on nectar and pollen in flowering trees and nest in a eucalypt hollow. The live Birds in Backyards page is still filed as Trichoglossus haematodus. **Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoo** *Zanda funerea*  verdict: n/a, tier: 
- trees: Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoos feed on hard native seeds and pine cones, and they nest in a large eucalypt hollow. Birds in Backyards and the Australian Museum say they favour eucalypt woodland and pine plantations, eat seeds of native trees and pine cones, plus some ground-plant seeds and insects, and nest in a large tree hollow lined with wood chips. BirdLife Australia says the older foods are banksia, hakea and casuarina seeds, and insect larvae in wattle branches, and that Monterey Pine cones are now a major food. Wikipedia's feeding account names Drooping Sheoak (Allocasuarina verticillata), Silver Banksia (Banksia marginata), wattles, and introduced Pinus radiata and a cypress, Cupressus torulosa. Nests are large hollows in tall eucalypts, and roosts are tall emergent eucalypts. Drooping Sheoak, Silver Banksia and several wattles are named for Inverleigh, and River Red Gum and Manna Gum are the local eucalypts. Indexed Leigh News text says sheoak cones are used by cockatoos and parrots, without naming this species. No 5 km record says which tree the birds were feeding in, and pine feeding at Inverleigh is not documented.
- hangouts: Within 5 km of Inverleigh, the Atlas of Living Australia holds 50 records of this species, and no locality string has more than 3. The highest are Hamilton Highway at Native Hut Creek, Murgheboluc (3) and Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve (3). Old Shelford Track at Carrah Track, Old Shelford Track between Common Road and Carrah Track, Inverleigh–Winchelsea Road between Thomas Road and Gnarwarre Road, and Lawson Reserve each have 2. Single records include High Street, the Barwon River south of town, and the misspelt Inverleifh Common. The counts are too sparse to name a favourite local spot.

### Grok batch 9 (grok-4.7, prompt docs/research/prompt9.txt, output batch9.json)

**Koala** *Phascolarctos cinereus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 5km
- trees: DEECA names the eucalypts preferred by koalas in Victoria as Manna Gum (Eucalyptus viminalis), Swamp Gum (E. ovata), Blue Gum (E. globulus) and River Red Gum (E. camaldulensis). It says they feed almost exclusively on eucalypt leaves, a low-energy diet, and are sedentary most of the day (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). Wildlife Victoria says they mainly eat eucalypt leaves but will also take acacia, melaleuca and corymbia, and that a koala typically uses only a couple of local species out of more than 800 eucalypts (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/koalas/). The Australian Museum says the diet is leaves of certain eucalypts plus some flowers and stems (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/). At Cape Otway, a different part of Victoria, DEECA describes over-browsing of Manna Gum and says over-abundance there is tied to the koalas' reliance on that tree (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas/koalas-at-cape-otway). For the Barwon country, Koala Clancy Foundation says River Red Gum is the main browse tree in the You Yangs and Little River and is probably also the most preferred koala tree in the Moorabool and Barwon river systems (https://koalaclancyfoundation.org.au/what-we-plant-for-koalas-and-why/). In a February 2024 letter the same foundation says koalas in the Teesdale and Bannockburn country love River Red Gum and Swamp Gum beside creeks and on the flats, and Manna Gum, Yellow Box (Eucalyptus melliodora) and Yellow Gum (Eucalyptus leucoxylon) on the sandy plains (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/koalas-in-need-of-accommodation/). A May 2023 Golden Plains Times report of their planting between Inverleigh and Bannockburn lists river red gum, manna gum, yellow box, yellow gum, silver wattle and black wattle, and quotes the president saying koalas in the Inverleigh common are not living with enough trees (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/tree-effort-for-koalas-returns/). The Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve page confirms Manna Gum and River Red Gum as the dominant trees there, and does not mention Swamp Gum, Blue Gum, Yellow Box or Yellow Gum (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). No ALA or iNaturalist record opened for this batch names the tree a local koala was in. Shelter trees are the same food trees in the DEECA account (mature trees for food and shelter). Koala Clancy's general planting notes say koalas on hot days often use leafy non-eucalypts such as Blackwood for shade; that note is not an Inverleigh observation (https://koalaclancyfoundation.org.au/what-we-plant-for-koalas-and-why/).
- hangouts: Distances below are from -38.10, 144.05, calculated from the public coordinates. Inside 5 km the named places are versions of one reserve. ALA locality strings and dates: Inverleigh Flora Reserve, three Victorian Biodiversity Atlas rows on 3 December 1991 at -38.06127, 144.03491 (about 4.5 km north-north-west), with individual counts 4, 8 and 4, which should not be added together; Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve, 15 July 2015, about 3.7 km, uncertainty 50 m, duplicated in the Geelong Field Naturalists Club; Inverleigh Flora & Fauna Reserve code IFFR40, 26 January 2002, about 4.9 km; Inverleigh Common, 8 January 2016 (Teesdale VIC 3328 Inverleigh Common in the VBA) about 4.8 km, and 16 March 2017 about 3.9 km, each duplicated between the VBA and the field naturalists; Inverleigh Native Cons Reserve, Teesdale, 10 November 2021, about 3.8 km, uncertainty 418 m, the same point as iNaturalist observation 103941110; OLD SHELFORD TK 0.75K NW OF CARRAH TK 5.2K S OF TEESDALE, 8 December 1998, and ROUGHLY 4 KM NNW OF INVERLEIGH, 27 January 1999, share the coordinate -38.07497, 144.04234 (about 2.9 km); ROUGHLY 4 KM S OF TEESDALE, 6 July 1989, about 4.8 km. A 30 September 1986 VBA record is labelled only Inverleigh, at -38.10684, 144.05967, about 1.1 km from the town centre, with 900 m uncertainty, so it is not a named street or reserve. The Friends page says koalas are seen occasionally in the Nature Conservation Reserve (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). iNaturalist research-grade records inside 5 km are https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/103941110 (10 November 2021, place guess Inverleigh Teesdale Rd, Teesdale, description 'vehicle strike, rescue') and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/44939192 (5 May 2020, place guess Inverleigh VIC 3321, public accuracy about 2.3 km, so the point is only a general location; the VBA copy says 'Centre about Inverleigh VIC ( 4km)'). Just outside 5 km but inside 10 km, three research-grade records have the place guess Inverleigh VIC 3321 and no finer public locality: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/263127183 (8 February 2025, description 'Mature female', accuracy 851 m, about 5.1 km), https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/408168580 (10 October 2026, about 5.8 km; not yet in the ALA extract), and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/173176918 (15 July 2023, accuracy 150 m, about 5.9 km, description 'Sheep?'). East of town, Bannockburn Bush has a 30 October 2019 record of two koalas at about 9.6 km, duplicated in the VBA and the Geelong Field Naturalists Club. Nearby iNaturalist research-grade points are https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/42374591 (25 May 2017, place guess 'Bannockburn Reerve', accuracy 802 m, about 9.0 km) and three 2023 Bannockburn VIC 3331 records, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/146446702 (7 January), https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/149101093 (19 February) and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/167005592 (11 June), about 9.6 to 9.8 km. Two 6 July 1989 VBA rows are labelled ROUGHLY 5 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE and ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE; their coordinates sit beside the later Bannockburn Bush point. A February 2024 letter says a mature male was seen in Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve in January 2023, and that scratches have been seen at Woolbrook and in the reserve (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/koalas-in-need-of-accommodation/). That January 2023 reserve sighting is not among the ALA or iNaturalist records pulled for this circle.

It is not a feeding study at Inverleigh.
  - Swamp Gum, Blue Gum, Yellow Box and Yellow Gum are not named on the Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve plant page. The reserve page names Manna Gum and River Red Gum as the dominant trees.

Three VBA rows on 3 December 1991 at one Flora Reserve point carry counts of 4, 8 and 4. They are the same day and the same coordinate and must not be added up.

- origins:
  - The koala is a marsupial in the family Phascolarctidae, genus Phascolarctos, species cinereus (Australian Museum, https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/, updated 28 July 2026). It is endemic to Australia. The approved conservation advice for the EPBC-listed entity says the species is conventionally Phascolarctos cinereus (Goldfuss 1817), that three subspecies were once described including P. c. victor for Victoria, and that there is no genetic evidence for those subspecies (https://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/85104-conservation-advice-12022022.pdf, in effect 12 February 2022). Southern animals are the larger, longer-furred form: the same advice gives an average male weight of 12 kg in Victoria against 6.5 kg in Queensland, and DEECA says Victorian males can weigh up to 15 kg and females up to 11 kg, with longer thicker fur than Queensland koalas (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas, page last updated 2 September 2026). Nothing opened for this batch says whether the Inverleigh animals descend from a particular translocation.
- distribution:
  - The Australian Museum maps a patchy distribution from northern Queensland to southern Victoria and south-eastern South Australia (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/). The 2022 conservation advice says the species also occurs in the ACT, that the listed threatened entity is only the combined populations of Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT, and that other populations in Victoria and South Australia are not listed under the EPBC Act. It describes the species as widespread in lowland and foothill eucalypt forests and woodlands across Victoria, and says southern populations are robust, with overpopulation and active control in some places (Menkhorst 2008, cited there). It also records translocations to French, Phillip, Raymond and Snake islands in Victoria, and reintroductions within the natural range on mainland Victoria (https://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/85104-conservation-advice-12022022.pdf). DEECA says koalas are widespread through eucalypt woodlands and forests in lowland Victoria and that the state has a large population, close to half a million, while some places hold very high densities (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). Zoos Victoria says southern koalas inhabit low-altitude forests and woodlands across central and southern mainland Victoria and on Raymond, Snake, French and Phillip islands (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/koala-forest/southern-koala/). Around Inverleigh the Atlas of Living Australia holds 19 records inside 5 km (1986–2021) and 33 inside 10 km (1983–2025) of -38.10, 144.05 (biocache queries listed under queries). A February 2024 letter from Koala Clancy Foundation in the Golden Plains Times says sightings in Inverleigh and Teesdale, and along the Moorabool downstream from She Oaks, are scarce, that the 1980s had many records and each decade since has had fewer, and that the foundation also knows of reports at Maude, Russells Bridge and Gheringhap (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/koalas-in-need-of-accommodation/). Those extra place names were not matched to coordinates inside the 10 km circle in this pass. The foundation's 2022 Inverleigh page estimates 2 to 10 koalas left in the population it mapped, isolated mostly in Inverleigh Flora Reserve (https://www.koalaclancyfoundation.org.au/lifeline-for-inverleigh-koalas/). That figure is the foundation's estimate, not a DEECA census.
- habitat:
  - DEECA says Victorian koalas live in eucalypt woodlands and forests in the lowlands, and that they need many healthy mature trees for food and shelter (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). Wildlife Victoria says the habitat of choice in Victoria is tall eucalypt forest and woodland through southern and central Victoria, and that populations are concentrated in small areas because of habitat destruction and urbanisation (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/koalas/). The Australian Museum says the koala lives in eucalypt forests and spends most of its time in eucalypt trees, sometimes travelling on the ground (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/). At Inverleigh, the Friends of the Nature Conservation Reserve say the reserve is about 1,050 ha between Inverleigh and Teesdale, that koalas are seen occasionally, and that the dominant trees are Manna Gum (Eucalyptus viminalis) and River Red Gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis), with Hedge Wattle (Acacia paradoxa) the main large shrub and Wallaby Grass on the ground (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). The same page says only about 1% of Victoria's former grassy woodlands remain and that two-thirds of that remainder is this reserve, classed as an endangered ecological vegetation class. The Golden Plains planning scheme Significant Landscape Overlay schedule 16 describes the Leigh River (Waywatcurtan) meeting the Barwon at Inverleigh, with riparian River Red Gum (Biyal), Yarra Gum, Blackwood and Black and Silver Wattle; the animals it names there are platypus, Great Egret, crayfish and Growling Grass Frog, not the koala (https://planning-schemes.app.planning.vic.gov.au/Golden%20Plains/ordinance/42.03-s16). Corangamite CMA's Grassy Eucalypt Woodlands Stewardship Program covers private-land woodland from Shelford east to the You Yangs, south to Inverleigh and north to Meredith. The animals named on that page are Fat-tailed Dunnart, Striped Legless Lizard, Golden Sun Moth and Growling Grass Frog, not the koala (https://ccma.vic.gov.au/projects/grassy-eucalypt-stewardship-program/).
- trees:
  - DEECA names the eucalypts preferred by koalas in Victoria as Manna Gum (Eucalyptus viminalis), Swamp Gum (E. ovata), Blue Gum (E. globulus) and River Red Gum (E. camaldulensis). It says they feed almost exclusively on eucalypt leaves, a low-energy diet, and are sedentary most of the day (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). Wildlife Victoria says they mainly eat eucalypt leaves but will also take acacia, melaleuca and corymbia, and that a koala typically uses only a couple of local species out of more than 800 eucalypts (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/koalas/). The Australian Museum says the diet is leaves of certain eucalypts plus some flowers and stems (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/). At Cape Otway, a different part of Victoria, DEECA describes over-browsing of Manna Gum and says over-abundance there is tied to the koalas' reliance on that tree (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas/koalas-at-cape-otway). For the Barwon country, Koala Clancy Foundation says River Red Gum is the main browse tree in the You Yangs and Little River and is probably also the most preferred koala tree in the Moorabool and Barwon river systems (https://koalaclancyfoundation.org.au/what-we-plant-for-koalas-and-why/). In a February 2024 letter the same foundation says koalas in the Teesdale and Bannockburn country love River Red Gum and Swamp Gum beside creeks and on the flats, and Manna Gum, Yellow Box (Eucalyptus melliodora) and Yellow Gum (Eucalyptus leucoxylon) on the sandy plains (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/koalas-in-need-of-accommodation/). A May 2023 Golden Plains Times report of their planting between Inverleigh and Bannockburn lists river red gum, manna gum, yellow box, yellow gum, silver wattle and black wattle, and quotes the president saying koalas in the Inverleigh common are not living with enough trees (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/tree-effort-for-koalas-returns/). The Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve page confirms Manna Gum and River Red Gum as the dominant trees there, and does not mention Swamp Gum, Blue Gum, Yellow Box or Yellow Gum (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). No ALA or iNaturalist record opened for this batch names the tree a local koala was in. Shelter trees are the same food trees in the DEECA account (mature trees for food and shelter). Koala Clancy's general planting notes say koalas on hot days often use leafy non-eucalypts such as Blackwood for shade; that note is not an Inverleigh observation (https://koalaclancyfoundation.org.au/what-we-plant-for-koalas-and-why/).
- hangouts:
  - Distances below are from -38.10, 144.05, calculated from the public coordinates. Inside 5 km the named places are versions of one reserve. ALA locality strings and dates: Inverleigh Flora Reserve, three Victorian Biodiversity Atlas rows on 3 December 1991 at -38.06127, 144.03491 (about 4.5 km north-north-west), with individual counts 4, 8 and 4, which should not be added together; Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve, 15 July 2015, about 3.7 km, uncertainty 50 m, duplicated in the Geelong Field Naturalists Club; Inverleigh Flora & Fauna Reserve code IFFR40, 26 January 2002, about 4.9 km; Inverleigh Common, 8 January 2016 (Teesdale VIC 3328 Inverleigh Common in the VBA) about 4.8 km, and 16 March 2017 about 3.9 km, each duplicated between the VBA and the field naturalists; Inverleigh Native Cons Reserve, Teesdale, 10 November 2021, about 3.8 km, uncertainty 418 m, the same point as iNaturalist observation 103941110; OLD SHELFORD TK 0.75K NW OF CARRAH TK 5.2K S OF TEESDALE, 8 December 1998, and ROUGHLY 4 KM NNW OF INVERLEIGH, 27 January 1999, share the coordinate -38.07497, 144.04234 (about 2.9 km); ROUGHLY 4 KM S OF TEESDALE, 6 July 1989, about 4.8 km. A 30 September 1986 VBA record is labelled only Inverleigh, at -38.10684, 144.05967, about 1.1 km from the town centre, with 900 m uncertainty, so it is not a named street or reserve. The Friends page says koalas are seen occasionally in the Nature Conservation Reserve (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). iNaturalist research-grade records inside 5 km are https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/103941110 (10 November 2021, place guess Inverleigh Teesdale Rd, Teesdale, description 'vehicle strike, rescue') and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/44939192 (5 May 2020, place guess Inverleigh VIC 3321, public accuracy about 2.3 km, so the point is only a general location; the VBA copy says 'Centre about Inverleigh VIC ( 4km)'). Just outside 5 km but inside 10 km, three research-grade records have the place guess Inverleigh VIC 3321 and no finer public locality: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/263127183 (8 February 2025, description 'Mature female', accuracy 851 m, about 5.1 km), https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/408168580 (10 October 2026, about 5.8 km; not yet in the ALA extract), and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/173176918 (15 July 2023, accuracy 150 m, about 5.9 km, description 'Sheep?'). East of town, Bannockburn Bush has a 30 October 2019 record of two koalas at about 9.6 km, duplicated in the VBA and the Geelong Field Naturalists Club. Nearby iNaturalist research-grade points are https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/42374591 (25 May 2017, place guess 'Bannockburn Reerve', accuracy 802 m, about 9.0 km) and three 2023 Bannockburn VIC 3331 records, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/146446702 (7 January), https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/149101093 (19 February) and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/167005592 (11 June), about 9.6 to 9.8 km. Two 6 July 1989 VBA rows are labelled ROUGHLY 5 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE and ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE; their coordinates sit beside the later Bannockburn Bush point. A February 2024 letter says a mature male was seen in Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve in January 2023, and that scratches have been seen at Woolbrook and in the reserve (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/koalas-in-need-of-accommodation/). That January 2023 reserve sighting is not among the ALA or iNaturalist records pulled for this circle.
- breeding:
  - DEECA says koalas breed from September to March, one young is born after a pregnancy of 33 to 35 days, the joey stays in the pouch for about six months, then rides on the mother's back until weaning at about one year (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). Wildlife Victoria says the mating season runs from August to March, that it usually receives reports of aggressive behaviour, loud calls and sometimes injury or exhaustion of the female in that season, that there is usually one joey a year, that the joey is in the pouch for about six months and independent at about one year, and that the joey must eat the mother's pap to gain the gut microbes that digest eucalypt leaf (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/koalas/). The Australian Museum says breeding occurs during summer and usually one joey is produced each year, and that after six months in the pouch the joey is weaned from milk onto leaves and pap (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/). Zoos Victoria says the call is a bellow (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/koala-forest/southern-koala/). No Inverleigh record opened here is of a joey or of a birth date. DEECA and Wildlife Victoria disagree by a month on when the season starts, so the local page should not collapse them into one date.
- diet:
  - Leaves of a few local eucalypts, low in energy, so the animal rests most of the day. DEECA says Victorian koalas prefer Manna Gum, Swamp Gum, Blue Gum and River Red Gum, are active for about four hours, usually after dark, and usually walk on the ground between trees (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). Wildlife Victoria says adults eat 0.5 to 1 kg of leaves a night and may sleep for up to 20 hours, and that they also sometimes eat acacia, melaleuca and corymbia (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/koalas/). Zoos Victoria says they spend about 18 to 20 hours sleeping and are mainly nocturnal (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/koala-forest/southern-koala/). The Australian Museum adds some flowers and stems, and a long caecum for the fibrous leaf (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/). Which of those trees the Inverleigh animals actually eat is not in the occurrence records. The local woodland that matches the DEECA list is Manna Gum and River Red Gum in the Nature Conservation Reserve (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/), and the foundation's account of River Red Gum, Swamp Gum, Manna Gum, Yellow Box and Yellow Gum in the Teesdale–Bannockburn country (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/koalas-in-need-of-accommodation/).
- threats:
  - DEECA says Victoria's population is currently secure but faces habitat loss and fragmentation, climate change, bushfire, drought and disease, that koalas are prone to heat stress and dehydration, and that dogs and vehicle collisions are further threats. Fragmented habitat matters because the low-energy diet leaves little spare energy for travel between food trees (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). The same page asks drivers to notice koala road signs, slow down, and take extra care at dawn and dusk. That is statewide advice. Searches for a koala warning sign on the Hamilton Highway at Inverleigh did not find a published source, so this file does not say such a sign is there. A local vehicle strike is documented: iNaturalist observation 103941110, 10 November 2021, description 'vehicle strike, rescue', place guess Inverleigh Teesdale Rd, Teesdale, about 3.8 km from the town centre, accuracy 418 m, and the VBA locality for the same point is Inverleigh Native Cons Reserve, Teesdale (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/103941110). Wildlife Victoria says the most common koala reports it receives are animals hit by a vehicle, animals on the ground, and animals displaced from habitat, and that koalas are also at risk from oxalate nephrosis, mange, chlamydia and retrovirus (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/koalas/). The 2022 conservation advice treats vehicles, dogs, chlamydia, koala retrovirus, drought and heatwaves as threats to the listed northern populations, and says Victorian and South Australian populations are in a different position, including overpopulation in some places (https://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/85104-conservation-advice-12022022.pdf). No source opened here reports chlamydia, mange or heat deaths in the Inverleigh animals. Habitat loss locally is the foundation's account: clearing for farming and housing, an estimate that 87% of habitat in its map area has gone, and a planting program because koalas in the Inverleigh common do not have enough trees (https://www.koalaclancyfoundation.org.au/lifeline-for-inverleigh-koalas/ and https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/tree-effort-for-koalas-returns/). The February 2024 letter says the cause of fewer sightings is not known, and that a drying and warming climate is the likely cause (https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/goldenplains/news/koalas-in-need-of-accommodation/). The reserve page also records off-road vehicles and thickets of Hedge Wattle as problems in the reserve, but it does not tie those problems to koalas (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/).
- conservation:
  - The EPBC listing is the combined populations of Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory, listed Endangered with effect from 12 February 2022. The conservation advice says populations in Victoria and South Australia are not part of that listed entity and are not listed (https://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/85104-conservation-advice-12022022.pdf). The Australian Museum page, updated 28 July 2026, says the same: koala populations in New South Wales, Queensland and the ACT are Endangered under the EPBC Act (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/). DEECA's koala facts paragraph still says the EPBC listing is Vulnerable in those three jurisdictions (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas, page last updated 2 September 2026). That sentence is the 2012 category. The 2022 advice is the later instrument. A search of the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act Threatened List, July 2026, for Koala, Phascolarctos and cinereus found no koala entry. The only cinereus hits were Xenus cinereus and Alectryon subcinereus (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf). The koala is therefore not on the current Victorian threatened list. Zoos Victoria's southern koala page says koalas are Vulnerable in Queensland, NSW and the ACT and Near Threatened in Victoria (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/koala-forest/southern-koala/). Near Threatened is that page's wording. It is not an FFG category. DEECA says Victoria has a large, thriving population and that in some areas high densities defoliate preferred food trees. Management is set out in the Victorian Koala Management Strategy (May 2023), whose themes include overpopulation, rehabilitation, genetics, disease, habitat, population knowledge, climate and fire, plantations, and community views. The strategy page says close to half a million koalas live in Victoria and that the population still faces disease, climate change and poor genetic diversity (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas). At Cape Otway, DEECA runs programs because koalas over-browse Manna Gum (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas/koalas-at-cape-otway). A May 2023 summary of the strategy, retrieved via search index of the DEECA PDF, names Cape Otway, French Island and Raymond Island as places where koalas can reach unsustainable densities (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0030/633576/Final_VKMS_Summary_May_2023.pdf). Inverleigh is not named on those pages. The local story in the sources above is a small, sparse population in remnant grassy woodland, not an overabundance site. Golden Plains Shire publishes a Koala Habitat polygon dataset, based on a 2006 study, described as a koala overlay aimed at keeping native vegetation that koalas use for food, shelter and movement (https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/golden-plains-koala-habitat, updated 9 August 2023). This pass did not find a planning-scheme schedule with that title. What was read in the ordinance near Inverleigh is ESO4, the Inverleigh remnant vegetation area, which protects mature remnant trees, Clover Glycine and the link to the Nature Conservation Reserve, and does not name the koala (https://planning-schemes.app.planning.vic.gov.au/Golden%20Plains/ordinance/42.01-s4), and SLO16 on the Leigh, which also does not name the koala. The IUCN Red List page was not opened.
- safetyAndWhatToDo:
  - Do not approach or handle a koala. Wildlife Victoria says to stop only if it is safe, assess from a distance, and call its 24/7 Emergency Response Service on (03) 8400 7300. A koala that has climbed a tree after a strike may still need a vet. A koala that stays on the ground, or walks slowly, is a reason to call. If a koala is in a garden tree and looks uninjured, keep dogs and other pets away and tell neighbours with dogs; it may move on in a day or two, or take up to 24 hours if dogs have been present (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/koalas/ and https://www.wildlifevictoria.org.au/news/safety-on-roads). The reporting page is https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/report-a-wildlife-emergency/. DEECA says to slow where koala road signs are posted, especially at dawn and dusk, give an animal on the road time to move, restrain dogs, and report a sick or injured koala to the nearest wildlife shelter. Its Customer Service Centre is 136 186, and it points people to the Help for Injured Wildlife tool (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas and https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/injured-native-wildlife/help-for-injured-wildlife). Better Health Channel has no koala fact sheet. Its bushfire-aftermath page says not to try to catch injured wildlife, and to call DEECA on 136 186 for wildlife carers (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bushfire-aftermath-safety-tips). A search of betterhealth.vic.gov.au for koala did not return a koala page. On the road, Wildlife Victoria says never step into traffic and, on freeways, its volunteers do not attend alone and the case is reported to 000 (https://www.wildlifevictoria.org.au/news/safety-on-roads).
- notWellDocumented:
  - No occurrence opened for this batch names the tree species a koala was sitting in at Inverleigh, Teesdale or Bannockburn. Preference for Manna Gum, River Red Gum, Swamp Gum and Blue Gum is the statewide DEECA list, plus Koala Clancy Foundation's account of the Barwon and Moorabool. It is not a feeding study at Inverleigh.
  - Swamp Gum, Blue Gum, Yellow Box and Yellow Gum are not named on the Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve plant page. The reserve page names Manna Gum and River Red Gum as the dominant trees.
  - The Koala Clancy Foundation estimate of 2 to 10 koalas, and of 87% of habitat gone inside its map, is the foundation's 2022 appeal text. It is not a DEECA or ALA population count. Three VBA rows on 3 December 1991 at one Flora Reserve point carry counts of 4, 8 and 4. They are the same day and the same coordinate and must not be added up.
  - Several ALA rows are the same sighting in two datasets (VBA plus Geelong Field Naturalists Club, or VBA plus iNaturalist). The published totals, 19 inside 5 km and 33 inside 10 km, count those rows separately.
  - The January 2023 mature male reported in the Nature Conservation Reserve is in a February 2024 letter. It is not in the ALA year facets (latest inside 5 km is 2021; the 2023 ALA rows inside 10 km are iNaturalist points at Bannockburn and one Inverleigh point on 15 July 2023) and it was not in the iNaturalist research-grade pull.
  - Reports of koalas at Maude, Russells Bridge, Gheringhap, Woolbrook and along the Moorabool below She Oaks come from that letter. Their coordinates were not verified inside the 10 km circle.
  - iNaturalist observation 41870720 (26 September 2018) is research grade but obscured, with a public accuracy of about 28 km. Its public coordinate is not a place. Two casual observations inside the 10 km search, 195147651 and 201334892, are also obscured. They are not hangouts.
  - The 5 May 2020 point has a public accuracy of about 2.3 km and the VBA text 'Centre about Inverleigh VIC ( 4km)'. It is not a precise tree or street.
  - The 1983 and 1988 VBA records labelled Teesdale use one coordinate with 4.5 km uncertainty, about 6.7 km north of the town centre. They are not a precise Teesdale hangout. The 1986 record labelled only Inverleigh has 900 m uncertainty.
  - An ALA row from Earth Guardians Weekly Feed, October 2018, sits about 9.1 km east and has no locality string in the extract. It is not used as a named place.
  - No published source found in this pass places a koala road sign on the Hamilton Highway at Inverleigh. DEECA's advice about koala signs is general. The documented local vehicle case is the 10 November 2021 iNaturalist record described as a vehicle strike and rescue, with a place guess of Inverleigh Teesdale Road and a VBA locality of the nature conservation reserve.
  - No local survey of chlamydia, mange, heat stress or dog attack at Inverleigh was found. Those threats are statewide or northern-population sources.
  - DEECA says koalas are not territorial and have overlapping home ranges of about 1.2 to 1.7 ha in ideal habitat. Wildlife Victoria says they are territorial and mark with chest glands. Both pages were read. They are not reconciled here.
  - Breeding start month differs: DEECA September, Wildlife Victoria August, Australian Museum summer. No Inverleigh breeding record was found.
  - The Museums Victoria Eastern Kulin seasonal calendar page did not load, so a search snippet about Gurrborra mating in Poorneet season was not used.
  - The IUCN Red List assessment page was not opened. Zoos Victoria's 'Near Threatened in Victoria' is not the FFG status. The July 2026 FFG list does not contain the koala.
  - DEECA's koala facts still say the EPBC status is Vulnerable. The conservation advice in effect from 12 February 2022, and the Australian Museum page updated 28 July 2026, say Endangered for Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT only.
  - The Golden Plains Koala Habitat dataset describes a koala overlay from a 2006 study. No planning-scheme schedule of that name was opened. ESO4 and SLO16 near Inverleigh do not name the koala.
  - The Great Victorian Koala Survey section on the DEECA page still says results will be available in 2025, on a page last updated 2 September 2026. This pass did not find a published result for Inverleigh.
  - A direct fetch of the Victorian Koala Management Strategy summary PDF returned a Cloudflare block via curl. The Cape Otway, French Island and Raymond Island overabundance line is from the search-index text of that PDF, not a full read of the file. The live DEECA HTML pages for koalas and for Cape Otway were opened.
  - A search snippet of the Corangamite CMA 2025–26 Moorabool seasonal watering proposal mentions koalas and a Lethbridge anecdote of animals moving to the river in hot months. That PDF was not opened page by page, Lethbridge was not measured inside the 10 km circle, and the anecdote is not used as an Inverleigh record.
  - Better Health Channel returned no koala page. The only wildlife-rescue guidance used from it is the bushfire-aftermath page, which is about injured wildlife in general.

  - {"url": "https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/koala/", "title": "Koala — Australian Museum", "accessed": "2026-10-25", "supports": "Updated 28 July 2026. Family Phascolarctidae, size 68–82 cm, eucalypt forests, patchy range from northern Queensland to southern Victoria and south-eastern South Australia, EPBC Endangered in NSW, Queensland and the ACT, diet of certain eucalypt leaves plus some flowers and stems, breeding in summer, usually one joey, pap after six months in the pouch."}
  - {"url": "https://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/85104-conservation-advice-12022022.pdf", "title": "Conservation Advice for Phascolarctos cinereus (Koala) combined populations of Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory", "accessed": "2026-10-25", "supports": "In effect 12 February 2022. Listed entity Endangered. Victoria and South Australia populations are not listed. Species widespread in lowland and foothill eucalypt forest and woodland in Victoria. Southern populations described as robust, with control programs where overpopulated. Former subspecies including P. c. victor not supported genetically. Threats named for the listed population include drought, heatwaves, vehicles, dogs, chlamydia and KoRV. Average Victorian male about 12 kg."}
  - {"url": "https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas", "title": "Koalas — DEECA wildlife.vic.gov.au", "accessed": "2026-10-25", "supports": "Page last updated 2 September 2026. Widespread in lowland Victorian eucalypt woodland and forest. Preferred trees Manna Gum, Swamp Gum, Blue Gum and River Red Gum. Breeding September to March, gestation 33–35 days, one joey, pouch about six months, weaned at about one year. Males up to 15 kg, females up to 11 kg. Threats: habitat loss and fragmentation, climate change, bushfire, drought, disease, heat stress, dogs, vehicles. Advice to heed koala road signs, drive carefully at dawn and dusk, restrain dogs, and call 136 186 or use Help for Injured Wildlife. Victorian Koala Management Strategy, close to half a million koalas, over-browsing where densities are high. Facts paragraph still says EPBC Vulnerable, which is older than the 2022 Endangered listing. Survey section still says results will be available in 2025."}
  - {"url": "https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/koalas/koalas-at-cape-otway", "title": "Koalas at Cape Otway — DEECA", "accessed": "2026-10-25", "supports": "Over-abundance at Cape Otway linked to reliance on Manna Gum, reluctance to change food source, climate and a lack of predators.   - {"url": "https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0030/633576/Final_VKMS_Summary_May_2023.pdf", "title": "Victorian Koala Management Strategy summary, May 2023", "accessed": "2026-10-25", "supports": "Search-index text only. **Snake safety around Inverleigh** *None*  verdict: n/a, tier: None
- hangouts: Use the species objects for places inside 5 km and in the 5–10 km ring. This object only records the nearest evidence for the snakes that are not in those tiers, so they are not dropped into Inverleigh by expectation. Tiger snake: zero ALA and zero iNaturalist inside 10 km. Nearest ALA is Museums Victoria, Bannockburn, Saffin Court, 17 November 2024, about 11.8 km. Nearest open iNaturalist point is Donaldson Road, Lethbridge, 11 October 2026, about 16.6 km. Other tiger snake points inside 25 km on iNaturalist are around 22–25 km (Fyansford, Highton, Newtown, Lovely Banks, Gherang), including roadkill. One research-grade observation, 203092052, says the snake was killed by a domestic animal; it is location-obscured, about 22 km on the public coordinate, and is not a place. Red-bellied black snake: zero inside 20 km on ALA and on iNaturalist. Nearest ALA is about 28.4 km, 'roughly 2 km west of Fairy Park', December 1989. Research-grade iNaturalist clusters around Staughton Vale and Brisbane Ranges National Park, about 31 km and beyond. White-lipped snake: one ALA record at about 18.3 km on the Mount Mercer–Shelford road at Shelford, April 2018, and zero iNaturalist inside 25 km. It is not given a species object because it is outside 10 km. iNaturalist at 50 km, all grades, also returned one boomslang (Dispholidus typus) and one Children's python (Antaresia childreni). Both disappear from the research-grade counts. They are not treated as wild Inverleigh snakes. Obscured little whip snake coordinates inside 5 km and 10 km are counted and are not mapped.
- Not well documented:
  - Tiger snakes and red-bellied black snakes are widely expected, and Better Health Channel and DEECA name them as common Victorian snakes. They have no ALA or iNaturalist record inside 10 km of -38.10, 144.05. That is an absence of records, not a survey that proves absence.
  - The nearest tiger snake is about 11.8 km away at Saffin Court, Bannockburn, a museum specimen. The coordinate is to three decimal places and has no uncertainty field. It is not an Inverleigh sighting.
  - The nearest red-bellied black snake is about 28.4 km away, west of Fairy Park, in 1989. Fairy Park and the Brisbane Ranges are not Inverleigh hangouts.
  - The white-lipped snake at Shelford is about 18.3 km away. It is outside the tier and has no full species write-up.
  - iNaturalist at 50 km included a boomslang and a Children's python in all-grades counts only. They are not treated as local wild snakes.
  - Yellow-bellied sea snakes in the 50 km ALA facet are not Inverleigh records.
  - Python, blind snake, colubrid and boa family searches were 0 out to 50 km. DEECA's two Victorian pythons are not in this extract.
  - Obscured iNaturalist coordinates must not be turned into streets or reserves. Six of seven little whip snake observations inside 5 km are obscured.
  - ALA and iNaturalist double-count the iNaturalist Australia records. The published ALA totals already include them.
  - The July 2026 FFG Excel guessed URL failed earlier. The conclusion that these species are not on the threatened list is from a text search of the July 2026 PDF, which did load.
  - The IUCN Red List website was not opened for these species.
  - No Corangamite CMA snake-management page was found to cite. No Golden Plains species list names which snakes live at Inverleigh. The Gazette notice is shire-wide.
  - A childcare snake procedure on the shire website names taipans and death adders as Australian examples. Those species are not in the ALA radii used here, and that procedure is not used as a local fauna list.
  - Cat bite signs and a pet pressure-bandage method were not in the sources opened.
  - Wildlife Victoria's snake FAQ page returned 'page not found' when opened.
  - Museums Victoria species HTML was blocked or incomplete on direct fetch. Biology cited to those URLs is from indexed page text plus, for the Australian Museum, saved page text.

**Lizard-friendly garden** *None*  verdict: n/a, tier: None
- hangouts: Named places that the records actually use are Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve or Inverleigh NCR, Inverleigh Conservation Reserve, Old Teesdale Track, Old Shelford Track, Inverleigh Common, the town place guesses Inverleigh VIC 3321 and Teesdale VIC 3328, Bannockburn and Bannockburn Bush, Harvey Road paddocks, Mason's Road with 900 m uncertainty, Spring Creek Road for one blue-tongue roadkill, and '7 km S of Inverleigh' for White's skink. Obscured iNaturalist coordinates are not hangouts. Tile grids at the repeated Bannockburn coordinate -38.052582, 144.134824 are survey shelters. No new spot is added.
- Not well documented:
  - No local snail-bait death, cat attack or mower injury was found. The threats are the museum, Wildlife Victoria and DEECA accounts, plus one roadkill.
  - The DEECA species sheet says cats indoors at night. The protecting-wildlife page says keep the cat indoors. Both are cited and not merged into a single rule.
  - Direct download of the DEECA blue-tongue PDF returned HTTP 403. The sentences are indexed text of that URL.
  - Tile counts at Bannockburn must not be summed into a population.
  - The Pseudemoia row is an unresolved form. It is not a species profile.
  - The resident blue-tongue has no coordinate.
  - No Golden Plains Shire lizard page was found.

**Legless lizard or snake** *None*  verdict: n/a, tier: None
- hangouts: No legless-lizard hangout inside 10 km. The nearest named striped legless lizard places are Boonderoo Nature Conservation Reserve at Teesdale, about 14.8 km, and coarser points further out. They are listed on the striped-legless-lizard object and are not Inverleigh.
- Not well documented:
  - No legless lizard of any genus was returned inside 10 km. Absence in the databases is not a promise that one will never be seen.
  - The Land for Wildlife eyelid sentence is not a reliable test for pygopodids, which have a spectacle.
  - Ear, flap and tongue are the published differences, and the newsletter says they are not obvious when the person is startled.
  - The Hooded Scaly-foot exception is not a local record.
  - SPRAT HTML was 403. The ear, tongue and tail sentences are indexed text of that profile.
  - Do not handle the animal to confirm the characters.

### Grok batch 12 (grok-4.7, prompt docs/research/prompt12.txt, output batch12.json)

**Platypus** *Ornithorhynchus anatinus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 5km
- trees: Named tree species not stated. Sources describe native bank vegetation, roots, logs and stream shading rather than a preferred food tree (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/).
- hangouts: Named places on the ALA rows inside 5 km are the Leigh River at Inverleigh, the Barwon River at Inverleigh, and the confluence of the Barwon and Leigh Rivers. Close examples: GAP_SiteID FOTB23 Leigh River at about 0.3 km (2021, genetic water samples); Leigh River Inverleigh at about 0.5 km (2016); a platypus-survey point on the Leigh River in 2002; GAP_SiteID 99 Barwon River at about 1.1 km (2021); Barwon River: Inverleigh (1966, 900 m uncertainty); Barwon River: S of Inverleigh (1997); the confluence (cPlatypus, 2020 and 2022, about 1.5 km); and GAP_SiteID 25 Leigh River at about 3.4 km (2021), with a 2026 Australian Platypus Conservancy observation at the same upstream area. A 2025 cPlatypus note says the animal was seen at the end of Park Street. A 2023 note says it was close to the west bank beside a walking track. A 2023 row at about -38.1043, 144.0638 is a watched dive at late afternoon or dusk. iNaturalist 224575712 (24 June 2024, research, about 0.6 km, place guess Inverleigh) and 97751600 (10 October 2021, casual, about 2.2 km, accuracy 15 m) are the two observations inside 5 km. Golden Plains SLO16 names the platypus on the Leigh River (Waywatcurtan) where it meets the Barwon at Inverleigh (https://planning-schemes.app.planning.vic.gov.au/Golden%20Plains/ordinance/42.03-s16). Corangamite CMA says the Barwon flows near Inverleigh and the Leigh joins the Barwon there, and that the river is platypus habitat (https://ccma.vic.gov.au/projects/barwon-flagship-waterway/; https://ccma.vic.gov.au/waterways/waterway-management/water-for-the-environment/upper-barwon-river/). The 2024–25 water-year review records platypus citizen science at Inverleigh; it also names Winchelsea, which is outside this circle (https://ccma.vic.gov.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Water-year-review-Upper-Barwon-River-2024-25-V2.pdf). Also nearby, outside 5 km: GAP_SiteID FOTB 10 Barwon at about 6.3 km (eight repeated 2021 genetic samples); GAP_SiteID 24 Leigh at about 6.5 km; Murgheboluc at about 8.0 km (1978). Mount Pollock (1965) has 9000 m uncertainty and is not a site. A 2025 pair labelled Surf Coast LGA sits near -38.1475, 143.9926, about 7.3 km out; the LGA text is not the place. Fyansford and the Platy Patch are outside 10 km and are not used.

**Grey-headed Flying-fox** *Pteropus poliocephalus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 10km
- trees: Camp trees are described generally rather than as a single species. Wildlife Victoria: more than 100 species of native trees, plus introduced trees; favourite blossoms are eucalypts, and also paperbarks, grevilleas and banksias; garden figs and lilly pilly are eaten. Australian Museum: fruit, especially figs; nectar and pollen, especially gum trees. A Museums Victoria phrase “coastal stringybark” was on a collections page that was not fully reopened, so it is not used as a measured habitat claim. Curlwaa, NSW, is an AFD locality for a colony, not a local viewing site.
- hangouts: No row inside 5 km. All five ALA rows are March 2020, dataset SA Fauna, protocol sign-satellite tracking, count 1, uncertainty 5 m, recorded by Van Weenen, Meade, Martin and Welbergen, and none has a locality string. Distances from the centre are about 5.3, 5.6, 7.1, 8.4 and 9.6 km. Coordinates are -38.05858, 144.01898; -38.08045, 143.99078; -38.03700, 144.06240; -38.02653, 144.07353; and -38.01858, 144.01208. This file does not assign those fixes to a town, a street or a camp. Wildlife Victoria names camps at places such as Geelong, which is outside this circle, and says temporary camps follow food (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/grey-headed-flying-fox/). No Inverleigh camp was found on the pages opened. There is no iNaturalist observation inside 10 km.
- Not well documented:
  - Supplied ALA 0/5 matches. iNaturalist returned 0. All five rows are March 2020 satellite fixes with no locality. They are not a camp.
  - Wingspan is 'over 1 m' on the Australian Museum page and 'up to one metre' on the DEECA and Wildlife Victoria pages. Weight up to 1.1 kg is the DEECA figure. They are not merged into one number.
  - Birth timing differs in detail between DEECA, the Australian Museum and Wildlife Victoria.
  - SPRAT HTML returned a challenge to a direct download. The Vulnerable category and 6 December 2001 effective date are from the search index of the SPRAT page plus the August 2026 EPBC extract. The July 2026 FFG list was read as text and says Vulnerable.
  - Geelong camps named by Wildlife Victoria are outside 10 km.
  - Access date for this dossier: 2026-10-25. The EPBC Vulnerable category and the effective date 06-Dec-2001 are from the search-indexed SPRAT snippet for taxon_id=186, matched by Wildlife Victoria’s statement that the national listing was in 2001. The environment.gov.au host returned HTTP 403 to a direct fetch, so measurements or recovery-plan text from an unopened SPRAT page are not quoted. FFG category is Vulnerable for Victoria on the July 2026 list and on the Wildlife Victoria flying-fox page. Among the eleven species in this array, only Pteropus poliocephalus appears on that FFG Threatened taxa sheet. Other Victorian bats on the sheet (not in this set) include forms of Miniopterus orianae, Nyctophilus corbeni, Rhinolophus megaphyllus megaphyllus and Saccolaimus flaviventris. Yarra Bend and Wurundjeri Country are names printed on the Wildlife Victoria flying-fox page. Camp census figures from the unopened “Victoria’s flying-fox camps” page are omitted. Places named only as photo credits (Bunurong Country, Gunaikurnai Country, Dja Dja Wurrung Country) are not presented as survey sites. No local site was added unless the opened page named it. That is a town-centroid geocode, not a GPS site, and '2 km NW' is the text, not a mapped tree. The Australian Faunal Directory distribution states are New South Wales and Queensland only, and the IBRA regions do not include Victoria (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Vespadelus_pumilus). The Australian Museum page for the species describes a northern forest bat (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/bats/eastern-forest-bat/). This record is treated as a likely misidentification of another Vespadelus, not as evidence of a local resident. No iNaturalist observation inside 10 km.

Vespadelus vulturnus, V. regulus and V. darlingtoni are the forest-bat species whose opened AFD pages include both Victoria and the Victorian Volcanic Plain; V. regulus and V. darlingtoni also include Tasmania on the States line, and V. vulturnus includes Victoria on the States line. No identification of a queried record is made. The Australian Museum eastern-forest-bat page has a map and no sentence placing the species in Victoria.

**Red fox** *Vulpes vulpes*  verdict: n/a, tier: 5km
- hangouts: Ten ALA rows inside 5 km and 19 inside 10 km. iNaturalist returned none at either radius. Named places inside about 5 km: Inverleigh NCR (an adult into 'A paradoxa' at 1.83 km in Sep 2022; another near the corner of Camp Tk and Old Teesdale Tk at 4.38 km in Sep 2020), Inverleigh Common near the golf course at 2.08 km in Aug 2021, Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve at 2.27 km in Jul 2010, the track string 'OLD SHELFORD TK 0.75K NW OF CARRAH TK 5.2K S OF TEESDALE' at 2.86 km in Mar 1999 (spotlighting on foot), and 'ROUGHLY 4 KM S OF TEESDALE' at 4.78 km in Jul 1989. Two foxScan points at 1.30 km (May 2021) and 2.02 km (Dec 2014) have no locality. One VBA row stores the coordinate 2.68 km away with locality 'Inverleigh', uncertainty 4,500 m, and an eventDate that parses to 1979-01-01 UTC while the year field is empty. That is the undated row in the year facet. It is the same coordinate as the 1979 cat record and is not a precise spot. In the outer ring: FeralScan points at 7.83, 8.71, 8.90, 9.06 and 9.68 km with no locality; Bannockburn (a fox across the road at 07:45 in May 2020); Bannockburn Bush (fox then a hare on the powerline track, nearer Harvey Rd than Old Base Rd, Feb 2020); Bannockburn Bush Reserve central block, west of Old Base Road and south of Bannockburn-Teesdale Road (scat analysis, Feb 2018, uncertainty 500 m); and 'ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE' (Jul 1989).
- Not well documented:
  - Ten and 19 are rows, not a population. Seven of the 19 are foxScan reports with no locality or count.
  - The 4,500 m 'Inverleigh' row is undated in the year facet. Its eventDate parses to 1979-01-01 UTC. It is not a precise hangout.
  - No local diet study. The $227.5 million figure and the $198 million lost-production figure are both national and are not combined.
  - The species page and the video disagree on whether foxes are reported in Tasmania.
  - The Victorian Fox Bounty page returned HTTP 403, so dollar amounts and closing dates are not reported.
  - iNaturalist has no fox observation inside 10 km. That is an absence of records, not proof of absence.
  - Corangamite CMA was not re-opened for a local fox prescription.

**European hare** *Lepus europaeus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 5km
- hangouts: Use the ALA Lepus capensis counts: 8 rows inside 5 km and 14 inside 10 km. They are not 8 or 14 animals. Three coordinate pairs inside 5 km are VBA plus Geelong Field Naturalists Club copies of one event: Inverleigh Golf Course, Nov 2019, count 4, at 2.29 km, remark 'Moving between Golf Course and nature reserve'; Inverleigh Common, Links track, Apr 2015, count 1, at 2.63 km; Inverleigh Common, Aug 2016, count 2, at 3.23 km. iNaturalist adds a research-grade Brown Hare at 4.39 km on 14 Feb 2025 (Rod Lowther, uncertainty 4 m, Inverleigh VIC 3321) and a casual one at 2.24 km on 20 Sep 2024, also place-guessed Inverleigh. The casual row is not in ALA. The third iNaturalist point inside the 5 km public radius is research grade but obscured (17 Oct 2018, place guess only 'Victoria, AU', ALA uncertainty 28,300 m). It is not a hangout. An Earth Guardians row at 7.97 km in Oct 2018 is the same QuestaGame user name BennyB and may be the same sighting under another coordinate. That link is not proven. Outer ring, 5-10 km: Bannockburn GFNC Apr 2022 at 7.75 km (the only raw name Lepus capensis); Teesdale iNaturalist Oct 2022 at 8.63 km and Mar 2022 at 9.03 km; Teesdale Grassy Woodland Reserve Sep 2021, two animals in grassland, at 8.75 km; 'ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE' Jul 1989 at 9.32 km; casual iNaturalist Bannockburn 11 Sep 2026 at 9.51 km, not in ALA.
- Not well documented:
  - ALA Lepus capensis and iNaturalist Lepus europaeus are the same local animal under two taxonomies. iNaturalist Lepus capensis is the Cape hare and returned 0 observations at 5 and 10 km.
  - User iNaturalist 3/6 is all grades. Research grade is 2/4 and matches the ALA iNaturalist Australia subset. Two casual rows (Inverleigh 2024 and Bannockburn 2026) are not in ALA.
  - Eight ALA rows inside 5 km collapse to three golf-course or common events plus two iNaturalist rows, one of which is obscured by 28.3 km.
  - The BennyB Earth Guardians coordinate and the obscured iNaturalist coordinate are not shown to be the same animal.
  - No Inverleigh damage measurement. The integrated hare page was HTTP 403.
  - Agriculture Victoria's further-reading link still titles one source Lepus capensis (Begnoche 2002). That does not change the name printed at the top of the Victorian page, which is Lepus europaeus.

**Black rat** *Rattus rattus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 5km
- hangouts: Six ALA rows inside 5 km and 11 inside 10 km. iNaturalist has none inside 5 km and one needs_id observation at Teesdale, 7.80 km, on 21 Sep 2024. Reserve records: Elliott trap, Mar 2018, tally 4, uncertainty 500 m, 'Inverleigh Conservation Nature Reserve Inverleigh', 2.20 km; found dead, Jul 2010, Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve, 2.27 km; cage trap, Oct 1988, tally 8, uncertainty 900 m, 'Inverleigh Common Flora Reserve', 4.87 km. An undated VBA row at 1.25 km has tally 10, uncertainty 900 m, protocol general observations, locality '2KM N; RUBBISH TIP'. The tally is not a population and the string is not evidence of a tip that is open now. OzAtlas rows by Trevor Pescott in Mar 2018 (tally 4 at 3.94 km with no locality, and tally 1 at 4.16 km) match the reserve trap date. They are not added to the reserve tally. Outer ring: Bannockburn Bush Reserve central block, Elliott trap, tally 3, Feb 2018, 9.25 km; camera, Bannockburn Bushland Reserve, Jul 2012, 9.42 km; 'ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE', Jul 1989, tally 1, 9.32 km; OzAtlas Oct 2017, tally 1, 9.11 km, no locality.
- Not well documented:
  - CaLP declaration was not confirmed. The species is absent from the established-invasive list that was read, and the gazette PDF returned HTTP 403.
  - The rubbish-tip locality is an undated row with 900 m uncertainty and a tally of 10. It is not a mapped tip and not a population.
  - OzAtlas Mar 2018 rows look like copies of the reserve Elliott-trap tally. They were not added and were not proven to be independent.
  - The one iNaturalist row is needs_id, not research grade.
  - Museum and health.vic body and weight ranges differ. Both are quoted. No local measurement exists.
  - No study of black-rat impact on native wildlife at Inverleigh. Museums Victoria's identification service page was not opened.
  - One native Rattus lutreolus row sits inside 10 km. Its locality was not downloaded.

**House mouse** *Mus musculus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 5km
- hangouts: Four ALA rows inside 5 km and seven inside 10 km. iNaturalist returned none at either radius. The clearest reserve record is an Elliott trap in Mar 2018, tally 11, uncertainty 500 m, at 'Inverleigh Conservation Nature Reserve Inverleigh', 2.20 km, the same point as a black-rat tally of 4. OzAtlas the same month has tally 11 at 3.94 km and tally 5 at 4.16 km, with no locality. The 11 is not counted again. Jul 1989 incidental, 'ROUGHLY 4 KM S OF TEESDALE', 4.78 km, count not filled. One FeralScan mouseScan point in May 2021 at 8.19 km has no locality. Outer VBA rows: Elliott trap, tally 1, Feb 2018, Bannockburn Bush Reserve central block, 9.25 km; incidental, tally 8, Jul 1989, 'ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE', 9.32 km.
- Not well documented:
  - Whether the house mouse is a declared established pest animal under the CaLP Act is unresolved here. The index lists the page, the species page does not say declared, and the duty list omits it. The gazette PDF was HTTP 403.
  - health.vic uses Mus domesticus. ALA and Agriculture Victoria use Mus musculus.
  - The Mar 2018 tally of 11 appears on a VBA reserve row and an OzAtlas row with no locality. They are not two populations.
  - Trap tallies are not mice per hectare. The 200 mice/ha rule of thumb is not a local density.
  - iNaturalist has no house mouse inside 10 km.
  - No Inverleigh plague record was found. The single mouseScan point has no locality.

**Cat (feral or domestic)** *Felis catus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 5km
- hangouts: Three ALA rows inside 5 km and five inside 10 km. iNaturalist returned none. The 1979 VBA row, locality '5' BLOCK CONTAINING MOUNT POLLOCK', uncertainty 4,500 m, stores a point 2.68 km from the centre. That is a five-minute block, not a pin on Mount Pollock. The two feralcatScan rows are rounded to one decimal degree (-38.1, 144.0 in Jul 2015 and -38.1, 144.1 in Aug 2019), both about 4.38 km away, with no locality. They are not hangouts. Outer rows: tally 2, Jul 1989, 'ROUGHLY 6 KM SW OF LOWNDE BRIDGE', 9.32 km; camera, tally 1, Jul 2012, Bannockburn Bushland Reserve, 9.42 km, uncertainty 500 m. Nothing in these rows separates a pet, a stray and a feral cat.
- Not well documented:
  - Five records do not separate feral, stray and owned cats. Two coordinates are rounded to 0.1 degree and one uncertainty is 4,500 m.
  - iNaturalist has no cat inside 10 km.
  - The shire page's 500,000 and 50,000 statewide figures are not tied to a study on that page and are not local counts.
  - The enclosure fee of $30.90 / $15.45 is printed against the April 2024 registration round. The current plan confirms a 50 percent discount only.
  - There is no cat curfew in the adopted 2026-2029 plan. Older web pages that mention a curfew should not be used.
  - National predation and disease figures are not Inverleigh measurements.
  - Museums Victoria, Zoos Victoria and Wildlife Victoria did not provide a cat-control page in this pass.

**Fallow deer** *Dama dama*  verdict: n/a, tier: 
- hangouts: No fallow deer record inside 5 km or 10 km on ALA (species facet and family Cervidae facet) or on iNaturalist taxon 42161. Nearest ALA rows are three, all 24.2-24.8 km south of -38.10, 144.05, in 2019, 2020 and 2021. The locality facet for that same 25 km search lists 'FA1_18 Gravel Pit Rd - 120m NW', 'Gharang Gherang Bushland Reserve', and 'Gherang Gherang Bushland Reserve ... off Forest Rd, near Anglesea, VIC'. The download did not join strings to coordinates. One remark, on the 24.4 km GFNC row, is three white deer browsing. Nearest iNaturalist row is casual, 24.7 km away, place guess 'Clarkes Rd, 1km S of Galatea Mine Rd, Anakie VIC 3213', on 13 May 2020. That is north of the centre, not the Anglesea cluster, and it is not Inverleigh. Inside 50 km ALA has 344 fallow rows. Locality labels that were returned include Stony Creek Reservoir Durdiwarrah, Brisbane Ranges National Park, Great Otway National Park, Lake Connewarre, Point Addis, Hospital Swamp and Otway Forest Park / Barwon Downs. None of those 80 labels names Inverleigh, Teesdale, Bannockburn, Shelford or Murgheboluc. They are not local hangouts.
- Not well documented:
  - Zero inside 10 km is an absence of records, not proof of absence.
  - The three ALA coordinates at 24.2-24.8 km were not joined to the three locality strings.
  - The Anakie iNaturalist observation is casual grade.
  - A taxon_name search for Dama dama without the taxon id falsely returned butterflies. Counts use taxon_id 42161.
  - Release history and a species-level field guide were not opened. Impact text is the statewide DEECA program, and the FFG threatening-process line is about Sambar.
  - 50 km locality labels do not include Inverleigh. A full coordinate download at 50 km returned HTTP 503, so the closest ALA fallow row inside that ring, beyond the three at 24 km, was not measured one by one.
  - FeralScan's deer page was not opened.

**Sambar** *Rusa unicolor*  verdict: n/a, tier: 
- hangouts: No Sambar record inside 5, 10, 25 or 50 km on ALA, under either Rusa unicolor or Cervus unicolor. iNaturalist has one research-grade Sambar at 25.14 km, on 11 Dec 2017, public coordinate about -37.906, 144.197, place guess '3221, , VIC, AU', accuracy 250 m, not obscured and not captive: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/9122439. That point is outside the 10 km tier and outside the 25 km search radius. It is not an Inverleigh hangout, and the postcode string is not turned into a suburb name here. Javan rusa, Rusa timorensis, is also absent from the ALA 50 km facet.
- Not well documented:
  - ALA and iNaturalist disagree at the 50 km scale: ALA 0, iNaturalist 1 research-grade row at 25.14 km. The observation was not found in the ALA species facet. Why it is missing from ALA was not established.
  - No Inverleigh record. Zero is not proof of absence.
  - No species biology page from Agriculture Victoria was opened, because Sambar is not on the established-pest list. Size and impact text are from the DEECA program page only.
  - The place guess is a postcode, not a verified locality name.

**Red deer** *Cervus elaphus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 
- hangouts: No red deer inside 5, 10 or 25 km on ALA or iNaturalist. Inside 50 km, ALA has 23 rows. Locality strings are Great Otway National Park ground-shoot sites, Forest Rd, Delaneys Rd in Otway Forest Park, Hurst Rd, Erskine Falls Rd, Deans Marsh Rd, Anglesea Heath and Iron Bark Basin at Point Addis. iNaturalist has four research-grade observations inside 50 km. The nearest public coordinate is 30.85 km, Bambra, on 8 Oct 2026 (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/409062072). The others are at Lorne (46.8 and 47.3 km) and Barwon Downs (48.2 km). Bambra, Lorne, Barwon Downs, the Otways, Anglesea and Point Addis are not Inverleigh hangouts. They are where the nearest public records actually are.
- Not well documented:
  - No record inside 25 km. The closest ALA row inside the 50 km ring was not measured because the coordinate download returned HTTP 503. The closest measured iNaturalist point is 30.85 km at Bambra.
  - Zero near Inverleigh is not proof of absence.
  - No Victorian species account of appearance or introduction was opened.
  - Ground-shoot location codes in the locality strings are record text from control programs. They are not invitations to visit those sites.

**Hog deer** *Axis porcinus*  verdict: n/a, tier: 
- hangouts: No Hog Deer row inside 5, 10, 25 or 50 km on ALA, and none inside 50 km on iNaturalist taxon 42165. No locality string in the deer facets names Inverleigh. There is no hangout to list. The nearest deer of any species in these pulls are fallow deer about 24 km south (ALA) and a casual fallow deer at Anakie about 24.7 km north (iNaturalist), plus one Sambar at 25.1 km. None of those is a hog deer and none is Inverleigh.
- Not well documented:
  - No record within 50 km on either ALA or iNaturalist. That is a strong absence in the public databases and still not a proof that the species has never occurred.
  - No species description or introduction history was opened from an allowed page.
  - iNaturalist's common name is Indochinese Hog Deer. The Victorian legal name used by DEECA and GMA is Hog Deer. They are treated as Axis porcinus.
  - Chital was empty at 50 km as well, which only means Axis axis also has no ALA row in that circle.

### 8e. Final merge, 26 Oct 2026, 5:45 AM AEDT
- All Grok batches 0–13 are merged, and `tsc --noEmit` passes.
- `birds.ts`: all 38 birds now have `trees`, `hangouts` and `tier`.
- New proposal files, not yet used by the site:
  - `content/mammals.ts`: 34 rows. That is the Koala, 23 native mammals and 10 introduced pests.
  - `content/reptiles.ts`: 14 rows. That is 3 snakes plus a safety entry, 6 lizards, Striped Legless Lizard (no local record), Eastern Snake-necked Turtle, a lizard-friendly garden entry and a legless-lizard-versus-snake entry.
- Koala appeared in both batch 9 and batch 12. I kept the batch 9 version.
- Batches 9–13 were able to open the July 2026 FFG list PDF. Batches 0–6 (the birds) could not, and used SPRAT/SWIFFT/the March 2025 list instead. Re-checking the bird FFG categories against the July 2026 PDF is still open.
